Blue Mountains.description: Part of the Greater Blue Mountains World Heritage Area since 2000, this is the most visited park in NSW. Its sandstone cliffs and deep valleys are best seen from lookouts such as Echo Point, home of the Three Sisters, and Govetts Leap.

Royal.description: Proclaimed in 1879, Royal was the first national park in Australia. Its 30 km Coast Walk runs from Bundeena to Otford, past sea cliffs, beaches like Garie and Wattamolla, and the Figure Eight Pools.

Ku-ring-gai Chase.description: Set aside in 1894, this park covers about 15,000 hectares of sandstone ridges and drowned river valleys where the Hawkesbury River meets Pittwater. It holds more than 800 Aboriginal heritage sites, and West Head lookout looks out over Broken Bay.

Lane Cove.description: Set aside in 1938, this 670-hectare park follows the Lane Cove River just 10 km from the Sydney CBD. Its riverside track is part of the Great North Walk and is popular with walkers, joggers and cyclists.

Kosciuszko.description: The largest park in NSW, at about 6,900 km², Kosciuszko contains Mount Kosciuszko, the highest peak on mainland Australia. It is also home to the Thredbo and Perisher ski resorts and part of the 655 km Australian Alps Walking Track.

Sydney Harbour.description: Created in 1975, this park protects 392 hectares of harbour headlands, beaches and islands. It includes historic sites such as Fort Denison and Bradleys Head, and lookouts at Dobroyd Head and Gap Bluff.

Brisbane Water.image_credit: Photo: NSW National Parks and Wildlife Service
Brisbane Water.description: This 11,500-hectare park of rugged sandstone country lies about 70 km north of Sydney on the Central Coast. Its walks range from easy to rugged, with lookouts such as Staples and Girrakool.

Morton.description: Covering almost 200,000 hectares of the Southern Highlands and South Coast, Morton is a park of waterfalls and cliffs. Highlights include Fitzroy Falls, Belmore Falls and the climb up Pigeon House Mountain (Didthul).

Bouddi.description: This small coastal park on the Central Coast, 93 km north-east of Sydney, reaches out into the Tasman Sea as a marine extension. It shelters Fletchers Glen, one of the last mature rainforests on the Central Coast, and headland lookouts such as Box Head.

Glenrock.description: Just 8 km south of Newcastle's city centre, this 534-hectare conservation area is best known for its mountain bike tracks. It also protects early coal-mining heritage sites, and has lookouts at Leichhardt and Dudley Beach.

Tomaree.description: Set up in 1984 at Port Stephens, about 150 km north-east of Sydney, Tomaree is known for its beaches and whale watching. On Tomaree Head you can still see gun emplacements built in 1941, during World War II.

Kamay Botany Bay.description: This park sits on the two headlands of Botany Bay, at La Perouse and Kurnell, where Captain Cook first landed in 1770 and Aboriginal people have lived for thousands of years. Cape Solander, on the Kurnell side, is a popular whale-watching spot.

Garigal.description: Gazetted in 1991, Garigal protects about 2,200 hectares of bushland 20 km north of the Sydney CBD. Its tracks, especially around the Cascades between Belrose and St Ives, are popular with bushwalkers and mountain bikers.

Eurobodalla.image_credit: Photo: NSW National Parks and Wildlife Service
Eurobodalla.description: Set up in 1995, this park stretches along the South Coast from Moruya Heads to Tilba Tilba Lake, south of Narooma. Its beaches, lakes and headlands support rich birdlife, with 131 species recorded.

Berowra Valley.description: A regional park from 1998 and a national park since 2012, Berowra Valley protects the bushland around Berowra Creek in Sydney's north-west. A 25 km stretch of the Great North Walk passes through it, and it has lookouts at Barnetts and Galston Gorge.

Worimi Conservation Lands.description: Owned and co-managed by the Worimi Aboriginal community with NPWS, these lands at Port Stephens include the Stockton Bight dunes, the largest moving coastal sand dunes in the southern hemisphere. Visitors come for beach driving, sandboarding and tours of Worimi cultural sites.

Illawarra Escarpment.description: Set up in 1980, this conservation area runs in six sections for about 40 km along the escarpment west of Wollongong. It is used for bushwalking, picnics, rock climbing, bird watching and taking in the views.

Coffs Coast.image_credit: Photo: NSW National Parks and Wildlife Service
Coffs Coast.description: This park links beaches and headlands along the coast around Coffs Harbour. The 60 km Solitary Islands coastal walk passes through it, and its headlands, such as Woolgoolga Headland, are good places to watch for whales.

Cape Byron.description: Walgun Cape Byron, just east of Byron Bay, is the most easterly point of mainland Australia. Its 1901 lighthouse sits at the top of a walking track lined with lookouts, a popular place to watch for whales.

Georges River.description: Set up in 1992, this 514-hectare park follows the Georges River 25 km south-west of the Sydney CBD. It is a local favourite for picnics, barbecues, boating and fishing.
